title: Minimum Window Subsequence
description: Brute force to optimized: testing every candidate substring directly versus a forward match scan paired with a backward tightening scan.

blocks.text: Given two strings S and T, return the minimum-length contiguous substring W of S such that T is a subsequence of W (T's characters appear in W in order, though not necessarily consecutively). If no such window exists, return an empty string. If multiple minimum-length windows exist, return the one starting at the leftmost position.

blocks.caption: Scan forward to find a valid window, then scan backward to shrink it to the tightest possible start

blocks.text: Given strings S and T, find the shortest contiguous stretch of S that contains every character of T, in order (as a subsequence, not necessarily adjacent), returning the leftmost such stretch if several share the minimum length.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Tightest Net That Still Catches Every Fish in Order
blocks.text: Like walking along a river spotting fish of specific species in a required order, and wanting to know the shortest stretch of riverbank from which every required species could be spotted in that order. First walk forward until every required species has been seen at least once, in order; then walk backward from that point to find exactly where the stretch could have started while still catching every fish in the right order.

blocks.caption: Each forward match is refined by a backward shrink, then the search resumes just past the shrunk window's start

blocks.text: Before checking every possible substring of S directly, notice that finding SOME valid window and then shrinking it is far cheaper than testing every candidate from scratch.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Scanning S forward with a second pointer into T, advancing that pointer whenever characters match, finds the EARLIEST point where a subsequence match of T completes, starting from any given position.

Observation 2: Once a match completes, the window found (from where the forward scan started matching, to where it just finished) may not be the TIGHTEST possible window ending at that same point, since some early characters used for matching earlier T-characters might not be strictly necessary.

Observation 3: Scanning backward from the match's end, matching T in REVERSE this time, finds exactly the tightest possible start for a window ending at that same point.

Observation 4: After recording this minimal window, the search must resume from just past the window's (possibly shrunk) START, not its end, since another, later match could start anywhere in between and potentially be even shorter or need comparing.

Recognizing that a forward "does a match exist" scan can be paired with a backward "how tight can it be" scan is the key two-pass technique that avoids ever testing an explicit candidate substring.
This is a two-pointer, two-pass technique: a forward pass to detect any valid match, followed by a backward pass to shrink it to the tightest window, repeated across the whole string.
For every possible starting position, extend the window forward until it becomes long enough to contain T as a subsequence, checking directly.

items: For every possible starting index, and every possible ending index at or after it, slice out the substring and directly check whether T is a subsequence of it.
The first (shortest) qualifying window found for each starting index is kept, since any longer window from that same start could never be shorter.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: isSubsequence is checked directly against each candidate window, since this brute force does not yet reuse any information between overlapping windows.
The inner loop breaks as soon as a qualifying window is found for a given start, since any longer window from that same start is never an improvement.
best is only updated when a strictly shorter qualifying window is found, keeping the leftmost one on ties since later, equal-length windows are simply skipped.

blocks.text: Every possible window is checked directly via a subsequence test, so the correct minimal window is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared * m) in the worst case, since each of roughly n squared candidate windows costs O(m) to verify as a subsequence match (where n = S.length, m = T.length).
Space: O(n) for building candidate substrings.

Limitation: checking every (start, end) pair directly ignores that a single forward scan can efficiently find the earliest completing match from a given point, and a backward scan can then find the tightest possible start, without ever materializing and testing individual substrings.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force tests every candidate window directly. Instead, scan S forward with a second pointer into T: whenever a character matches the next needed T character, advance that pointer; once all of T has been matched, a valid window has been found (though not necessarily the tightest one). Then scan backward from that point, matching T in reverse, to find the tightest possible start for a window ending there. Record this window if it beats the best found so far, then resume the forward scan from just past this window's start, since a better window could still begin nearby.

Maintain a pointer i scanning S and a pointer j scanning T. Whenever S[i] matches the currently needed T[j], advance j (and always advance i). Once j reaches the end of T, a match is complete: switch to a backward scan from the current position, matching T in reverse to find the tightest window start. Compare this window against the best found so far, then resume the forward scan from just past this window's start.
Alternate between a forward scan (to detect a complete subsequence match) and a backward scan (to shrink it to the tightest window), resuming just past each found window's start.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Both candidate windows have length 4; since "bcde" (starting at index 1) was found first and ties are resolved by keeping the earlier one, the final answer is "bcde".

codes.python:
def min_window(S, T):
    n, m = len(S), len(T)
    best_start, best_len = -1, float('inf')
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        j = 0
        if S[i] == T[j]:                                                     # found where a candidate match of T could start
            start = i
            while i < n and j < m:
                if S[i] == T[j]:
                    j += 1                                                   # advance through T as S is scanned forward
                i += 1
            if j == m:                                                       # all of T matched as a subsequence, ending just before i
                end = i
                j -= 1
                k = end - 1
                while j >= 0:                                                 # scan backward, matching T in reverse to find the tightest start
                    if S[k] == T[j]:
                        j -= 1
                    k -= 1
                window_start = k + 1
                window_len = end - window_start
                if window_len < best_len:
                    best_len = window_len
                    best_start = window_start
                i = window_start + 1                                        # resume the search just past this window's start
            else:
                break                                                        # not enough characters left in S to complete T
        else:
            i += 1
    return "" if best_start == -1 else S[best_start:best_start + best_len]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(min_window("abcdebdde", "bde"))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * m) in the worst case, since the forward and backward scans together advance through S a bounded number of times, each backward scan costing up to O(m).
Space: O(1) extra, beyond the returned substring itself.

The forward scan's job is only to detect THAT a valid subsequence match exists starting from some point, advancing through T greedily; the backward scan then finds exactly how tight that match's start can be, by re-matching T in reverse from the same ending point. Resuming the forward scan from just past the (possibly shrunk) window's start, rather than from the match's end, ensures overlapping candidate windows starting slightly later are never missed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Forward scan completes a full match of T","Switch to a backward scan to find the tightest window ending at that same point"],["Forward scan runs out of S before completing T","No further matches are possible; stop the search entirely"]]}

items: The forward scan advances i unconditionally every step, but only advances j when a character match occurs, correctly implementing a subsequence check.
The backward scan mirrors this logic in reverse, walking k backward and only advancing j (now decreasing) on a match, to find the tightest possible start.
i is reset to windowStart + 1 (not end + 1) after each found window, ensuring the search doesn't skip past potentially better overlapping windows.

blocks.text: Separating "does a match exist" (a forward scan) from "how tight can it be" (a backward scan) avoids ever needing to materialize and test individual candidate substrings directly.

items: Resuming the forward scan from the match's END instead of its (possibly shrunk) START, which can skip over better overlapping windows.
Forgetting the backward shrink step entirely, and using the forward match's starting point as the window's start, which can produce a longer-than-necessary window.

Not handling the "T cannot be fully matched" case, where the forward scan runs out of S before completing T, requiring the search to stop and return the best found so far (or empty, if nothing was ever found).

items: Explicitly separate the "forward: find A match" step from the "backward: find the TIGHTEST match" step when explaining the approach, since conflating them is a common source of confusion in this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Minimum window containing T as a SUBSEQUENCE (not all characters, in exact order)" points toward a forward-scan-then-backward-shrink two-pointer technique, distinct from the frequency-map sliding window used for "contains all characters of T" style problems.

items: How does this differ from the classic "Minimum Window Substring" problem? That problem only requires every CHARACTER of T to appear somewhere in the window (any order, via a frequency count); this problem requires T's characters to appear in the exact ORDER given, as a true subsequence.

How would you extend this to find ALL minimal-length windows, not just the leftmost? Continue the search after finding the first minimal window, comparing every subsequent complete match's tightened length against the current minimum, collecting all ties instead of discarding them.

What is the worst-case input that makes this run close to O(n * m)? A string S with a long run of the same repeated matching character for one T-position, forcing many backward-scan steps per forward match.

A two-pointer window technique, but distinct from the "frequency-map at-least/at-most" sliding windows used elsewhere in this category (Permutation in String, Minimum Size Subarray Sum), since matching a subsequence (ordered, not just present) requires this forward-then-backward two-pass structure instead.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared * m) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (forward match + backward shrink): O(n * m) time, O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: Two-pointer, two-pass technique: forward scan to detect a subsequence match, backward scan to shrink it to the tightest window
Core Idea: A forward pass finds THAT a match exists; a backward pass from the same endpoint finds exactly how tight its start can be
Time: O(n * m)
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: The forward scan's match start is not necessarily the tightest one; a backward re-match from the same end always finds the truly tightest start
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Match forward to find an end, then match backward from that end to find the tightest start
